concepts.name: NABARD: Establishment, Legal Basis and Ownership Structure
key_dimensions: Established under NABARD Act, 1981 — NOT under Companies Act or RBI Act
Commenced operations on July 12, 1982 by absorbing ARDC and refinance functions of RBI
Ownership: Government of India holds ~99% stake; RBI transferred its shares to GoI in 2010 (trap: many assume RBI still owns it)
Headquarters: Mumbai (trap: often confused with other development banks)

concepts.name: NABARD's Mandate and Functional Jurisdiction
key_dimensions: Apex development bank for agriculture, rural industries, small-scale industries, cottage and village industries, handicrafts
NOT a commercial bank — it does NOT directly lend to farmers (indirect lending via refinance)
Distinction between NABARD's promotional, developmental and supervisory roles
Overlap trap: NABARD vs SIDBI vs NHB — each apex institution for different sectors but similar refinance model

concepts.name: NABARD's Refinance Mechanism: Types and Eligible Institutions
key_dimensions: Short-term refinance (seasonal agricultural operations) vs Long-term refinance (investment credit for allied activities)
Eligible institutions: State Cooperative Banks, District Central Cooperative Banks, Regional Rural Banks, Commercial Banks, State Land Development Banks
NABARD does NOT provide direct credit to end-beneficiaries — this is a classic UPSC trap
Refinance vs Re-discounting: NABARD provides refinance, not re-discounting (RBI's tool)

concepts.name: NABARD and Supervision of Cooperative Banks and RRBs
key_dimensions: NABARD has statutory supervisory powers over State Cooperative Banks, District Central Cooperative Banks, and State Land Development Banks under NABARD Act
RRBs: NABARD supervises but RBI regulates — the supervision-regulation distinction is a frequent trap
Urban Cooperative Banks are supervised by RBI, NOT NABARD (common confusion)
NABARD conducts inspections under Section 35 of Banking Regulation Act for cooperative banks

concepts.name: Kisan Credit Card (KCC) Scheme and NABARD's Role
key_dimensions: KCC was introduced in 1998–99 based on recommendations of R.V. Gupta Committee — NABARD conceptualized and designed it
Provides revolving credit for crop cultivation, post-harvest expenses, allied activities and consumption needs
NABARD's role: Design and refinancing, NOT direct issuance (issued by commercial banks, RRBs, cooperative banks)
Recent extension: KCC extended to fisheries and animal husbandry farmers (PM-KISAN linkage)

concepts.name: NABARD's Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF)
key_dimensions: Established in 1995–96 within NABARD to fund rural infrastructure projects by state governments and panchayati raj institutions
Funded by shortfall contributions from scheduled commercial banks that fail to meet Priority Sector Lending (PSL) targets — critical linkage
RIDF does NOT cover urban infrastructure; confusion with AMRUT/Smart Cities is a trap
Types of projects: Irrigation, rural roads, bridges, flood protection, drinking water — NOT direct agricultural loans

concepts.name: Priority Sector Lending (PSL) and NABARD's Oversight Role
key_dimensions: NABARD monitors PSL targets for RRBs and cooperative banks; RBI monitors for commercial banks — jurisdiction trap
NABARD issues guidelines for agriculture sub-targets under PSL for RRBs
Shortfall in PSL by commercial banks → funds channeled to RIDF under NABARD
NABARD's Annual Rural Credit Plan (ARP) feeds into PSL planning at district level

concepts.name: NABARD and Self-Help Group–Bank Linkage Programme (SHG-BLP)
key_dimensions: Launched as pilot in 1992 by NABARD — world's largest microfinance programme
NABARD does not directly finance SHGs; it provides refinance to banks that lend to SHGs
Two models: SHG-Bank Direct Linkage vs SHG-MFI-Bank model — NABARD promotes both
NRLM (Aajeevika/DAY-NRLM) works alongside SHG-BLP but is a government programme under MoRD — not NABARD's scheme

concepts.name: NABARD and Microfinance: Role vs MUDRA and SIDBI
key_dimensions: NABARD refinances MFIs working in rural areas; MUDRA refinances MFIs for non-agricultural micro-enterprises — sector distinction
SIDBI manages MUDRA; NABARD manages rural microfinance — institutional overlap trap
NABARD's Micro Finance Development and Equity Fund (MFDEF) supports capacity building of SHGs and MFIs
NABARD does NOT regulate MFIs — RBI regulates NBFC-MFIs

concepts.name: NABARD's Watershed Development and Tribal Development Programmes
key_dimensions: NABARD implements Watershed Development Fund (WDF) for natural resource management in rainfed areas
Tribal Development Fund (TDF): Supports livelihood promotion of tribal households — NABARD-specific programme
Distinction: PMKSY (Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana) is a GoI scheme; WDF is NABARD's own fund — trap in attribution
NABARD uses these funds in partnership with state governments and NGOs, not as a direct implementer

concepts.name: NABARD's Annual Inspection and Credit Planning Functions
key_dimensions: Prepares Potential Linked Credit Plans (PLPs) for every district — basis for banks' Annual Credit Plans
PLPs identify sector-wise credit potential but are NOT binding on banks
NABARD's State Focus Papers consolidate district-level PLPs for state-level planning
Distinction: NABARD plans credit deployment; RBI sets monetary policy — functional boundary

concepts.name: NABARD Infrastructure Development Assistance (NIDA) and Long-Term Irrigation Fund (LTIF)
key_dimensions: NIDA: Direct lending by NABARD to state governments, state-owned entities for rural infrastructure — unlike RIDF, this is direct funding
Long-Term Irrigation Fund (LTIF): Announced in Union Budget 2016–17 under NABARD to fast-track incomplete major/medium irrigation projects
LTIF is funded through NABARD's market borrowings with GoI guarantee — not PSL shortfall funds (contrast with RIDF)
PMKSY–HKKP (Har Khet Ko Pani) projects are financed under LTIF — attribution trap

concepts.name: NABARD and Regional Rural Banks (RRBs): Ownership vs Supervision
key_dimensions: RRBs are owned by: Central Government (50%), Sponsor Bank (35%), State Government (15%) — NABARD does NOT own RRBs
NABARD supervises RRBs (inspection and monitoring) but does NOT regulate them — RBI issues regulatory guidelines
NABARD provides refinance and training support to RRBs through its regional offices
Recapitalization of RRBs is done by the three owners, not by NABARD — common misconception

concepts.name: NABARD's Role in Agricultural Credit Flow and Doubling Farmers' Income
key_dimensions: NABARD prepares annual assessment of agricultural credit flow targets in consultation with RBI and Ministry of Agriculture
Distinction: NABARD sets indicative targets for cooperative and RRB credit; RBI sets for scheduled commercial banks
Ashok Dalwai Committee (2017) on doubling farmers' income — NABARD is a key implementation agency
NABARD's refinance is concessional (below-market rates) to incentivize rural lending — this is a subsidy mechanism

concepts.name: NABARD Consultancy Services (NABCONS) and Capacity Building
key_dimensions: NABCONS is a wholly-owned subsidiary of NABARD providing consultancy in agriculture, rural development globally
Distinction: NABCONS is a commercial consultancy entity; NABARD itself is a development finance institution
BIRD (Bankers Institute of Rural Development) at Lucknow is NABARD's training arm — not a separate statutory body
NABARD Academy at Pune — training for NABARD officers and rural banking personnel

concepts.name: NABARD and Financial Inclusion: PM Jan Dhan and Beyond
key_dimensions: NABARD supports financial inclusion through refinancing BCs (Business Correspondents) of rural banks — indirect role
Financial Inclusion Fund (FIF) was merged from two funds (FITF and FIF) and is maintained by NABARD since 2016
FIF supports technology adoption, capacity building for financial inclusion — NOT direct cash transfer
Trap: PMJDY is managed by DFS (Ministry of Finance), NOT NABARD — NABARD supports rural infrastructure for inclusion

concepts.name: NABARD's Borrowing Powers and Resource Mobilization
key_dimensions: NABARD raises funds through: NABARD bonds (tax-free), market borrowings, GoI loans, RBI loans, external borrowings (ADB, World Bank)
NABARD can issue bonds to the public — these are sometimes tax-free under Section 10(15) of Income Tax Act
Bhavishya Nirman Bonds and Rural Bonds are NABARD instruments — distinct from government securities
NABARD's capital base is augmented by GoI contributions, NOT by SLR/CRR mechanisms (trap with RBI's tools)

concepts.name: NABARD and Agri-Business Development: FPOs and Agri Value Chain
key_dimensions: NABARD promotes Farmer Producer Organizations (FPOs) through equity grant support and credit guarantee under FPC Act 2013
Distinction: SFAC (Small Farmers' Agribusiness Consortium) also promotes FPOs under MoA&FW — dual agency trap
10,000 FPO scheme: Jointly implemented by NABARD, SFAC, and NCDC — not NABARD alone
NABARD's Agri-Business Finance Ltd (formerly NABFINS) provides microfinance in underserved areas of South India

concepts.name: NABARD vs SIDBI vs NHB: Apex Institution Comparison
key_dimensions: NABARD: Agriculture and rural development; SIDBI: Small and medium enterprises; NHB: Housing finance — sector-specific mandates
All three use refinance as primary tool and are NOT commercial banks — but NHB also directly lends to HFCs
Supervisory roles: NABARD supervises RRBs and cooperative banks; SIDBI supervises no banks; NHB regulates Housing Finance Companies
UPSC trap: NHB was a subsidiary of RBI, transferred to GoI in 2019 — parallels NABARD's 2010 ownership transfer from RBI

concepts.name: NABARD and Climate Finance: Green Initiatives and Sustainable Agriculture
key_dimensions: NABARD is an accredited National Implementing Entity (NIE) for Green Climate Fund (GCF) and Adaptation Fund — only Indian institution with dual accreditation
NABARD manages the National Adaptation Fund for Climate Change (NAFCC) on behalf of Ministry of Environment
Distinction: NAFCC is a GoI scheme implemented through NABARD; GCF projects are NABARD's own accredited programmes
NABARD's climate financing role is distinct from its traditional refinancing role — an emerging UPSC area
